lines.text:
The Architecture of Choice — How a Supermarket Works

A supermarket is designed to make you spend more time — and more money — than you intended. Every aisle, every shelf, every price tag is positioned according to decades of consumer psychology research. Understanding how a supermarket is organised is not just a vocabulary exercise — it is a lesson in how design shapes behaviour.

The layout follows a predictable logic. Fresh produce — apples, bananas, oranges, grapes, strawberries, tomatoes, lettuce, carrots, potatoes, onions — is placed at the entrance. The colours and textures create an impression of freshness and abundance. A scale allows customers to weigh loose items. Exotic fruits — mangoes, papayas, pomegranates, kiwis, figs — are displayed prominently, priced higher. Herbs — basil, thyme, rosemary, parsley, mint, cilantro, dill — sit nearby.

The dairy section — milk, cheese, yogurt, butter, eggs, cream, sour cream, cottage cheese, cream cheese — is placed at the back of the store. This is deliberate: milk and eggs are the most frequently purchased items, so placing them at the rear forces customers to walk past every other aisle. Along the way, they pass the bakery — bread, bagels, croissants, muffins, baguettes, sourdough, naan, pita — where the smell of fresh baking is itself a marketing tool.

The meat and fish counter — chicken, beef, pork, fish, salmon, tuna, lamb, shrimp, sausage, bacon — occupies one wall. A butcher cuts to order behind the deli counter. Frozen foods — frozen pizza, frozen vegetables, ice cream — line the freezer aisles.

The centre aisles contain shelf-stable goods. Canned soup, peanut butter, jam, ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, olive oil, tomato sauce, honey, maple syrup, broth, soy sauce, and hot sauce fill one aisle. Pasta, rice, noodles, couscous, quinoa, cereal, flour, oatmeal, and pancake mix fill another. Spices and seasonings — salt, pepper, sugar, cinnamon, garlic, oregano, cumin, paprika, turmeric, nutmeg, curry powder, vanilla extract — are grouped together. Baking supplies — baking soda, baking powder, brown sugar — sit alongside.

Snacks — chips, cookies, chocolate, candy, crackers, popcorn, nuts, granola bars, pretzels, trail mix, dried fruit — occupy high-traffic areas. Beverages — water, soda, coffee, tea, juice, lemonade, energy drinks, sparkling water, coconut water, smoothies — fill an entire aisle.

Household supplies — soap, detergent, sponges, paper towels, trash bags, bleach, dish soap, toilet paper, aluminum foil, plastic wrap — are separated from food. Personal care — shampoo, toothpaste, toothbrush, deodorant, lotion, sunscreen, conditioner, body wash, mouthwash, vitamins — occupies a quieter section.

At the checkout, a cashier scans each barcode. A conveyor belt moves items forward. A scanner reads prices. A receipt prints. A self-checkout machine offers an alternative. The express lane serves customers with fewer items. A loyalty card provides discounts. A coupon reduces the price. A sale sign announces offers. An expiration date tells you when to use the product. Nutrition facts list ingredients and calories.

Packaging varies by product: a can, a bottle, a box, a jar, a bag, a carton, a tube, a wrapper, a package, a container, a crate, a tray, a bunch, a loaf, a dozen, a pouch. Quantities are measured differently too — a pound of cheese, a gallon of milk, a bunch of bananas, a head of lettuce, a loaf of bread, a dozen eggs, a slice of cake.

The supermarket is a landscape of engineered persuasion — and the more you understand its architecture, the better you navigate it.

lines.text: 'Trolley' (BrE) = 'shopping cart' (AmE). 'Basket' is the same in both. In British supermarkets you often need a £1 coin to unlock a trolley (returned when you bring it back). American stores usually have free carts.
lines.name: 'Trolley' (BrE) = 'shopping cart' (AmE). 'Basket' is the same in both. In British supermarkets you often need a £1 coin to unlock a trolley (returned when you bring it back). American stores usually have free carts.

lines.text: 'Supermarket' is used in both BrE and AmE. 'Grocery store' or 'grocery' is more common in AmE. 'Corner shop' (BrE) = 'convenience store' (AmE) = a small local shop. 'Hypermarket' = a very large supermarket (common in Europe). 'Off-licence' (BrE) = 'liquor store' (AmE).

lines.text: In the UK, single-use plastic bags have been replaced by reusable 'bags for life' (usually 10p-20p each). Many shoppers bring their own bags. This is now common worldwide. 'Paper or plastic?' was a classic American checkout question.

lines.text: In Britain, queuing (waiting in line) is taken very seriously. Cutting the queue (jumping the line) is considered extremely rude. At self-checkout, there is usually one shared queue. In America, 'standing in line' follows similar etiquette but is less culturally iconic.

lines.text: 'Information' is uncountable — never 'an information' or 'informations.' Use: 'some information', 'a piece of information', 'the information.' Same pattern: 'advice' (not *an advice), 'news' (not *a news), 'research' (not *a research). The verb is 'inform': 'The sign informs customers about the sale.'

lines.text: 'Bread' is uncountable — use 'a loaf of bread', 'a slice of bread', 'some bread.' Never *'a bread.' 'A dozen' is followed directly by the noun: 'a dozen eggs' (not *a dozen of eggs). Compare: 'dozens of eggs' (with 'of' when 'dozens' is used as a vague quantity). Similarly: 'a hundred people' but 'hundreds of people.'

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer items', 'fewer customers', 'fewer aisles.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less sugar', 'less traffic', 'less time.' Common error: using 'less' with countable nouns. Note: supermarket signs that read '10 items or less' are grammatically informal — the standard form is '10 items or fewer.'

lines.text: Reported speech requires tense backshift when the reporting verb is past ('asked'). Present → past: 'want' → 'wanted', 'prefer' → 'preferred.' Full sequence: 'Do you want...?' → 'She asked if I wanted...' 'Will you pay...?' → 'She asked if I would pay...' No backshift needed if the reporting verb is present: 'She asks if I want a bag.'

lines.text: 'Be used to' + gerund (-ing) = accustomed: 'I'm used to going.' 'Used to' + infinitive = past habit: 'I used to go' (but I don't any more). 'Get used to' + gerund = becoming accustomed: 'I'm getting used to going.' Three distinct structures with different meanings — the gerund vs. infinitive choice changes the meaning entirely.
